tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

Kenneth Jiang Wed Oct 14 13:17:41 2026 +0000
Revert "Defer the project assistant's tools by default with hosted tool search"

This reverts commit 491b56d26b. Every tool is sent to the model loaded again,
as it was before.

With most tools hidden behind tool search, the assistant could not prepare a
print. The instructions name tools such as intent_update, presets_list,
object_analyze and plan_set. The model called them by name without searching
for them first, so it never saw their parameters, guessed the arguments, and
was refused. The third refusal in a turn ends the turn. In live runs of
scripted conversations (DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, every tool after
the first three deferred), 20 of 25 refused calls were such guesses, and no
attempt to prepare an outdoor PETG part ever reached a slice.

With every tool visible again, either by building with this commit reverted
or by turning deferral off, no turn was ended by refused calls in 36 runs of
the same conversations. On the prompt as committed, the assistant read the
part's shape before guessing what it was and found PETG in the printer's own
preset list. 4 of 9 attempts finished the preparation through slicing and
reading the slice report; the others were stopped by a separate slice_start
bug. The runs and how to repeat them are in
tests/project_journey/README.md, added in a following commit.

Deferral was only measured on OpenRouter with single-function deferral; the
built-in OpenAI route with namespaces was not tested. How to bring deferral
back without hiding the tools the instructions rely on is being investigated
separately.

# How these prompt experiments are run

Read this whole file before doing anything. Your own brief names your hypothesis and your arms; this file is the
method every experiment shares.

## What is being investigated

JusPrin is a 3D-printing slicer (an OrcaSlicer fork) with an in-app assistant that prepares prints by calling
tools. Two behaviours matter most to the product: choosing a filament and process that suit what the print is
for, and looking at the model, guessing what it is, confirming with the person, and preparing from that.
The assistant's instructions were built up piecemeal and do not get these reliably. We are finding out which
parts of the instructions cause which failures, one mechanism at a time.

The "journeys" are four scripted conversations run in the real app against a live model, whose tool calls the
app really answers. Read these, they are short:

- `C:\src\JusPrin\tests\project_journey\README.md` — what a journey is, what a record holds, the results so far.
- `C:\src\JusPrin\tests\project_journey\scenarios\*.json` — the four scenarios and their review questions.
  `outdoor-fitting` and `desk-ornament` should act; `petg-question` and `what-is-this` should only answer.

## The control

Every experiment is a change to the control, which is what the app sends today:

- `control-instructions.txt` (in this folder): the whole instructions text.
- `control-tools.json`: every tool, whether it is deferred, and its description. Parameter schemas are in
  `C:\src\JusPrin\src\slic3r\GUI\JusPrin\Agent\ToolRegistry.cpp` (read only; search for the tool's name).

Facts about this setup that results depend on:

- The model is DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter. It is text only: it cannot see the picture `view_render`
  returns, so do not steer it toward pictures.
- Only `settings_get`, `settings_search` and `workspace_inspect` are loaded. Every other tool is deferred:
  the model cannot see its name, description or parameters until it runs OpenRouter's hosted tool search
  (logged as `SEARCH`). A tool found in one user turn is not kept loaded in the next.
- A call with wrong arguments, or to a tool that does not exist, is refused and the model may try again. The
  third refusal in one turn ends the turn (`malformed_tool_call`). This limit is in the app, not the prompt.
- The harness has a printer preset selected but no printer set up in JusPrin, so the opening message
  sometimes asks which printer the person has. That is the fixture, not your experiment.

What the control did earlier today (a guide only, not your control): `earlier\rewrite` holds 12 records of
exactly this control, and `earlier\head-prompt` 12 of the prompt before it. The README's last results section
compares them. Every `outdoor-fitting` run so far ended on a third refused call before the project was sliced.

Your control is `shared-control\control`: 12 fresh records of the control, run in the same hours as your arms.
It is being produced while you work. Check `shared-control\control\_status.txt`; do not start your comparison
until it says `done`. Do not run the control yourself unless your brief says to.

## Making an arm

An arm is one JSON file in your own folder, `exp\<your experiment>\<arm>.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "search-first",
  "replace": [ { "find": "exact text in the control instructions", "with": "new text" } ],
  "instructions": "optional: the whole instructions text instead, for a rewrite",
  "toolDescriptions": { "plan_set": "optional: a new description for a tool" },
  "loaded": [ "optional: names of deferred tools to send loaded instead" ]
}
```

Prefer `replace`: it keeps the change small and attributable. Each `find` must occur exactly once in the
control text or the run refuses to start. An arm changes one mechanism. Two ideas are two arms.

## Running an arm

```
pwsh -File <exp>\run.ps1 -Experiment <your experiment> -Arm <arm> -File <exp>\<your experiment>\<arm>.json
```

It runs the four scenarios three times each (12 runs, about 20 to 30 minutes), one app at a time. Start it with
`run_in_background: true`, then call `pwsh -File <exp>\wait.ps1 -Experiment <x> -Arm <arm>` (it blocks up to
nine minutes; set the tool timeout to 600000) until it reports `ended`. Run your arms one after another, never
two at once: six experiments share this machine.

`-Scenarios a,b` limits the scenarios and `-Runs n` the repeats. A run that already has a record is skipped, so
an interrupted arm can simply be started again.

## Reading an arm

```
node <exp>\sent.mjs <record.json>                 what that run really sent (do this once per arm, first)
node <exp>\outcomes.mjs <arm dir> [<arm dir>...]  each run: calls in order, intent recorded, how it ended, totals
node <exp>\refused.mjs <arm dir> [...]            every refused call with the arguments the model sent
node <exp>\refused.mjs --responses <arm dir>      what each model response held, in order (SEARCH = tool search)
node <exp>\show.mjs <record.json>                 one whole conversation, replies and calls
```

## The method

1. **Predict before you run.** Write, in your report file, which outcomes your change should move, in which
   scenario, in which direction, and which must not move. Do this before the first run and do not edit it after.
2. **One mechanism per arm.** If an arm changes two things you cannot say which one worked.
3. **Compare against the same hours.** Your arms against `shared-control\control`. Earlier records are a guide.
4. **Three runs, large effects only.** 0 or 1 of 3 against 3 of 3, or a count that changes several-fold, is an
   effect. Anything smaller is "no visible effect", and say so. Do not buy more runs to rescue an unclear result.
5. **Outcomes, not paths.** An outcome is what the project ended as, what was recorded, and what the last reply
   claims. Which tool came first and how many calls it took is the path. Report both, labelled, and judge on
   outcomes.
6. **Both directions.** Each change is read on the scenario it targets and on its partner that should not
   change. A fix that helps one and breaks the other is not a fix.
7. **Attribute by mechanism.** For each thing that moved, name the sentence you changed that plausibly caused
   it and quote the evidence from a record: the call's arguments, the reply's words, the response items. Then
   say plainly what helped, what did not matter, and what hurt. A change that helps and hurts is two findings.
8. **Read the traces.** Read every failed turn and every refused call in your arms. Counts hide the reason.
9. **A failed run is a result.** Never rerun a run because it went badly, and never delete a record.
10. **No tuning loop.** Run the arms in your brief. You may add one more arm if a result directly suggests it
    and the budget allows; say why. Do not iterate wording until something passes.

## Limits

- **Spend:** one US dollar for your whole experiment. `run.ps1` counts what your folder has spent at list
  price and refuses to start a run past $0.90. If a provider error mentions a key or a quota, stop.
- **Touch nothing else.** Write only inside `exp\<your experiment>\`. Do not edit, build, commit or stage
  anything under `C:\src\JusPrin`. Do not read or print the keys file. Do not stop any process you did not
  start: other experiments' apps are running. Do not start other agents.
- **If the app will not start** (a run ends in seconds with no `LIVE USAGE` line in its log), read the end of
  that log, try the arm once more, and if it fails again stop and report what the log says.

## Your report

Write `exp\<your experiment>\REPORT.md` and return the same text as your final message:

1. The hypothesis, in one or two sentences.
2. Each arm: the exact text changed (before and after).
3. Your predictions, as written before running.
4. A table: each outcome you track, control against each arm, as counts out of 3.
5. What helped, what did not matter, what hurt, each tied to a sentence and to quoted evidence.
6. Your verdict on the hypothesis, and the wording you would keep.
7. Tokens and dollars spent, and anything that makes the result less trustworthy.

Keep it under 700 words plus the table. Say what you saw; do not round a weak result up.

# How these prompt experiments are run

Read this whole file before doing anything. Your own brief names your hypothesis and your arms; this file is the
method every experiment shares.

## What is being investigated

JusPrin is a 3D-printing slicer (an OrcaSlicer fork) with an in-app assistant that prepares prints by calling
tools. Two behaviours matter most to the product: choosing a filament and process that suit what the print is
for, and looking at the model, guessing what it is, confirming with the person, and preparing from that.
The assistant's instructions were built up piecemeal and do not get these reliably. We are finding out which
parts of the instructions cause which failures, one mechanism at a time.

The "journeys" are four scripted conversations run in the real app against a live model, whose tool calls the
app really answers. Read these, they are short:

- `C:\src\JusPrin\tests\project_journey\README.md` — what a journey is, what a record holds, the results so far.
- `C:\src\JusPrin\tests\project_journey\scenarios\*.json` — the four scenarios and their review questions.
  `outdoor-fitting` and `desk-ornament` should act; `petg-question` and `what-is-this` should only answer.

## The control

Every experiment is a change to the control, which is what the app sends today:

- `control-instructions.txt` (in this folder): the whole instructions text.
- `control-tools.json`: every tool, whether it is deferred, and its description. Parameter schemas are in
  `C:\src\JusPrin\src\slic3r\GUI\JusPrin\Agent\ToolRegistry.cpp` (read only; search for the tool's name).

Facts about this setup that results depend on:

- The model is DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter. It is text only: it cannot see the picture `view_render`
  returns, so do not steer it toward pictures.
- Only `settings_get`, `settings_search` and `workspace_inspect` are loaded. Every other tool is deferred:
  the model cannot see its name, description or parameters until it runs OpenRouter's hosted tool search
  (logged as `SEARCH`). A tool found in one user turn is not kept loaded in the next.
- A call with wrong arguments, or to a tool that does not exist, is refused and the model may try again. The
  third refusal in one turn ends the turn (`malformed_tool_call`). This limit is in the app, not the prompt.
- The harness has a printer preset selected but no printer set up in JusPrin, so the opening message
  sometimes asks which printer the person has. That is the fixture, not your experiment.

What the control did earlier today (a guide only, not your control): `earlier\rewrite` holds 12 records of
exactly this control, and `earlier\head-prompt` 12 of the prompt before it. The README's last results section
compares them. Every `outdoor-fitting` run so far ended on a third refused call before the project was sliced.

Your control is `shared-control\control`: 12 fresh records of the control, run in the same hours as your arms.
It is being produced while you work. Check `shared-control\control\_status.txt`; do not start your comparison
until it says `done`. Do not run the control yourself unless your brief says to.

## Making an arm

An arm is one JSON file in your own folder, `exp\<your experiment>\<arm>.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "search-first",
  "replace": [ { "find": "exact text in the control instructions", "with": "new text" } ],
  "instructions": "optional: the whole instructions text instead, for a rewrite",
  "toolDescriptions": { "plan_set": "optional: a new description for a tool" },
  "loaded": [ "optional: names of deferred tools to send loaded instead" ]
}
```

Prefer `replace`: it keeps the change small and attributable. Each `find` must occur exactly once in the
control text or the run refuses to start. An arm changes one mechanism. Two ideas are two arms.

## Running an arm

```
pwsh -File <exp>\run.ps1 -Experiment <your experiment> -Arm <arm> -File <exp>\<your experiment>\<arm>.json
```

It runs the four scenarios three times each (12 runs, about 20 to 30 minutes), one app at a time. Start it with
`run_in_background: true`, then call `pwsh -File <exp>\wait.ps1 -Experiment <x> -Arm <arm>` (it blocks up to
nine minutes; set the tool timeout to 600000) until it reports `ended`. Run your arms one after another, never
two at once: six experiments share this machine.

`-Scenarios a,b` limits the scenarios and `-Runs n` the repeats. A run that already has a record is skipped, so
an interrupted arm can simply be started again.

## Reading an arm

```
node <exp>\sent.mjs <record.json>                 what that run really sent (do this once per arm, first)
node <exp>\outcomes.mjs <arm dir> [<arm dir>...]  each run: calls in order, intent recorded, how it ended, totals
node <exp>\refused.mjs <arm dir> [...]            every refused call with the arguments the model sent
node <exp>\refused.mjs --responses <arm dir>      what each model response held, in order (SEARCH = tool search)
node <exp>\show.mjs <record.json>                 one whole conversation, replies and calls
```

## The method

1. **Predict before you run.** Write, in your report file, which outcomes your change should move, in which
   scenario, in which direction, and which must not move. Do this before the first run and do not edit it after.
2. **One mechanism per arm.** If an arm changes two things you cannot say which one worked.
3. **Compare against the same hours.** Your arms against `shared-control\control`. Earlier records are a guide.
4. **Three runs, large effects only.** 0 or 1 of 3 against 3 of 3, or a count that changes several-fold, is an
   effect. Anything smaller is "no visible effect", and say so. Do not buy more runs to rescue an unclear result.
5. **Outcomes, not paths.** An outcome is what the project ended as, what was recorded, and what the last reply
   claims. Which tool came first and how many calls it took is the path. Report both, labelled, and judge on
   outcomes.
6. **Both directions.** Each change is read on the scenario it targets and on its partner that should not
   change. A fix that helps one and breaks the other is not a fix.
7. **Attribute by mechanism.** For each thing that moved, name the sentence you changed that plausibly caused
   it and quote the evidence from a record: the call's arguments, the reply's words, the response items. Then
   say plainly what helped, what did not matter, and what hurt. A change that helps and hurts is two findings.
8. **Read the traces.** Read every failed turn and every refused call in your arms. Counts hide the reason.
9. **A failed run is a result.** Never rerun a run because it went badly, and never delete a record.
10. **No tuning loop.** Run the arms in your brief. You may add one more arm if a result directly suggests it
    and the budget allows; say why. Do not iterate wording until something passes.

## Limits

- **Spend:** one US dollar for your whole experiment. `run.ps1` counts what your folder has spent at list
  price and refuses to start a run past $0.90. If a provider error mentions a key or a quota, stop.
- **Touch nothing else.** Write only inside `exp\<your experiment>\`. Do not edit, build, commit or stage
  anything under `C:\src\JusPrin`. Do not read or print the keys file. Do not stop any process you did not
  start: other experiments' apps are running. Do not start other agents.
- **If the app will not start** (a run ends in seconds with no `LIVE USAGE` line in its log), read the end of
  that log, try the arm once more, and if it fails again stop and report what the log says.

## Your report

Write `exp\<your experiment>\REPORT.md` and return the same text as your final message:

1. The hypothesis, in one or two sentences.
2. Each arm: the exact text changed (before and after).
3. Your predictions, as written before running.
4. A table: each outcome you track, control against each arm, as counts out of 3.
5. What helped, what did not matter, what hurt, each tied to a sentence and to quoted evidence.
6. Your verdict on the hypothesis, and the wording you would keep.
7. Tokens and dollars spent, and anything that makes the result less trustworthy.

Keep it under 700 words plus the table. Say what you saw; do not round a weak result up.

77:## Skills versus tools
104:How something gets loaded into the model's context does not decide whether it is a skill or a tool. Today a skill costs its one line in the instructions, and a tool costs its definition on the first request of a conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). If we later use the model platform's deferred loading, both will cost one index line plus a load when needed. A skill could then be a deferred read-only tool: the tool's description is the skill's index line, and the tool's result is the skill's text. Tools and skills would then be found the same way and covered by the same eval.
106:## Prefer extending nouns over multiplying verbs
138:## Tool budget and tool shape
142:- OpenAI's function-calling guidance keeps fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn and defers the rest.
151:- `None` gives the model the full catalog from the start, as ordinary function calling. It is also how to turn deferral off.
152:- `Functions` turns on hosted search over functions that are deferred one by one.
153:- `Namespaces` turns on hosted search over deferred toolsets.
155:Deferral is on by default for the route the app ships with. When nothing is declared, `resolve_tool_search` gives the built-in model on the built-in endpoint `Namespaces`. That pair was checked live (see Deferral below). A different model or a different endpoint gets `None` until its own capability is declared, because nothing has been checked for it.
157:Any model on any compatible endpoint can use any mode it supports, without a code change. For a model or endpoint other than the built-in pair, declaring no capability keeps ordinary function calling. It does not make the model unavailable. When deferral is on, three reads stay loaded from the start: `workspace_inspect`, `settings_search`, and `settings_get`. This is a starting policy. It is not a measured ranking of how often each tool is called. Printer and filament sessions keep their small catalogs fully loaded. MCP is unchanged, because MCP clients do their own deferral.
178:Those cache hits are history. They lower the billed input cost. They do not remove definitions from the model's context, and they do not guarantee a hit on another request. The current catalog is over the 20-definition budget. Deferral targets the catalog's cost in the initial context while keeping the catalog stable. The live check under Deferral below gives the first figures for actual usage. Selection accuracy and latency across real tasks still need an approved live comparison.

---
name: windows-build-machine
description: "Facts about the Windows Server 2022 machine used for JusPrin Windows verification (no admin, RDP at 100%, no GPU, toolchain and Mesa locations)"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 1e908987-3ebc-4e47-9372-ca2af82d4fee
  modified: 2026-09-16T05:20:39.573Z
---

The JusPrin Windows verification box (Windows Server 2022, user `guitest`, as of 2026-09-09): no admin rights, no GPU, reached over RDP at 100% scaling. VS 2022 Build Tools, CMake and Ninja are installed; the deps live at `C:/src/JusPrin/deps/build/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local`. Main checkout `C:/src/JusPrin` is on `jusprin-newui` with a Release build in `C:/src/JusPrin/build`.

**Why:** Several handoff items were blocked on machine facts (no debugger, no admin, DPI cannot change from inside an RDP session), so knowing them up front saves a diagnostic pass.

**How to apply:**
- GL needs Mesa, and **every freshly configured CMake build tree starts without it** — nothing in CMake or the repo supplies it. Run `pwsh src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/windows-gl/provision-mesa-windows.ps1 -BuildDir <build dir> -Source C:\src\JusPrin\build\src\Release` after configuring; it copies `libgallium_wgl.dll` and `dxil.dll` (from `C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Redist\D3D\x64\`) beside every GUI exe and `opengl32.dll` into its `mesa\` subfolder. Placement is not interchangeable, and each missing file has a silent signature — both documented in "Software GL on Windows machines without a GPU" in `agent-docs/jusprin/engineering-method.md` (on `jusprin-newui` since 2026-09-13, commit `318208608f`).
- Quick recall of the signatures: no `libgallium_wgl.dll` → `glcontext not ready, postpone init`, no `got opengl version`, black canvas all session. No `dxil.dll` → d3d12 initializes, then exit `0x80070057` on the first canvas draw with nothing logged. Both verified by removing the file and re-running. With all three present, both `d3d12` (default, `4.2 … D3D12`) and `GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe` (`4.6 … llvmpipe`) render.
- `slow_bootup` only moves the dxil crash from startup to first canvas paint; it is not a workaround.
- Lesson: a clear-only WGL smoke test passed under d3d12 because clearing compiles no shader, and was wrongly read as clearing the driver. A smoke test that skips the suspect code path proves nothing about it. (That test was removed from the repo for this reason.)
- A first-run datadir (e.g. copies of `C:\b\dd3`) logs ~630k lines in the first minute — the `GuideFrame::GetFilamentInfo` profile scan, driver-independent. Not a GL symptom.
- `D3D12 (Microsoft Basic Render Driver)` in the log is **Mesa's own d3d12 gallium driver on WARP**, not Microsoft's GLon12 mapping layer and not a real GPU. Confirm which GL is live by listing the process's loaded modules: the bundled Mesa shows `<exe dir>\mesa\opengl32.dll` + `libgallium_wgl.dll` (+ `DXIL.dll` once d3d12 has drawn), the unprovisioned fallback shows only `C:\Windows\SYSTEM32\OPENGL32.dll`.
- The permission guard refuses `Remove-Item` under `C:\b` (it reports it as a protected path) and misparses `rd /s /q` and path-like string literals as delete targets. Hand build-tree deletion to the user; build trees there contain `resources` symlinks into live worktrees, so unlink those before any recursive delete.
- A debugger can be had without admin: download `https://aka.ms/windbg/download` (an .appinstaller pointing at a ~1.2 GB msixbundle), unzip the bundle, unzip `windbg_win-x64.msix`, and `amd64/cdb.exe` runs directly. Set `_NO_DEBUG_HEAP=1` when running the harness under cdb, or teardown crawls in the debug heap for many minutes.
- Fixture directories for the harness's visual modes must be short paths (e.g. `C:\Users\guitest\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\wp\...`); a long scratchpad path makes the profile-bundle copy exceed MAX_PATH and the fixture slice never validates.
- The harness prints everything on stderr; the exit code must be read with `$LASTEXITCODE` in PowerShell (bash shows 127).
- DPI at 150%/200% needs the user to reconnect the RDP session at that scale. See [[jusprin-windows-parity-handoff]].

Node is installed twice: the older `C:\tools\node` (v24.20.0), which is **not on PATH**, and
`C:\Users\guitest\.local\node-v24.21.0-win-x64` (v24.21.0, npm 11.19.0), added to the **user
PATH** on 2026-09-16. Check `Get-Command npm.cmd` before installing anything; a fresh Bash
session may still need `export PATH="$PATH:/c/Users/guitest/.local/node-v24.21.0-win-x64"`.

npm is not optional any more: since commit `5fc0efe2e3` the Agent and Home pages are built from
TypeScript and their `resources/jusprin/{agent,home}/index.html` is generated, not committed.
Without npm, CMake **fails at configure time** (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Web/CMakeLists.txt`
`FATAL_ERROR`), so the first new source file you add breaks the build tree; and without the
bundles the app creates no Agent WebView at all, which shows up as `shell_agent_webview_created
FAIL` / "the Agent page did not complete its handshake" in the shell harness. Build them with
`npm ci && npm run build` in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI` and `HomeUI`.

The shell harness and the Agent page must come from the same commit: a harness exe built before
a page change hangs at `agent_reply_streams_to_completion` instead of failing.

To work on `jusprin-mcp` (the MCP stdio helper) you do **not** need an app build, and a worktree
can have its own build tree in about three minutes: configure with `-DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF`
(skips the npm requirement above) plus
`-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=C:/src/JusPrin/deps/build/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local`, then
`cmake --build <dir> --config Release --target jusprin-mcp -- -m`, which compiles only the six
bridge/registry sources and `main.cpp`. `vswhere.exe` is **not** installed; vcvars is at
`C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\BuildTools\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvars64.bat`
and cmake at `C:\tools\cmake\bin\cmake.exe`. Point the Python suite at the result with
`JUSPRIN_TEST_BRIDGE=<dir>\src\Release\jusprin-mcp.exe`; the whole suite runs in ~8 s.

An **existing** build tree configured before node was installed keeps `JUSPRIN_NPM:FILEPATH=JUSPRIN_NPM-NOTFOUND`
in its CMakeCache, and `find_program` never retries a cached NOTFOUND -- so the next build fails at
configure with the `npm not found` FATAL_ERROR even once npm is on PATH. Reconfigure the tree once with
`cmake . -DJUSPRIN_NPM="C:/Users/guitest/.local/node-v24.21.0-win-x64/npm.cmd"`; putting node on PATH alone
is not enough. Neither the Bash tool nor a PowerShell session started before 2026-09-16 inherits the user
PATH entry, so prefix `$env:PATH` explicitly in each invocation.

**Shared build tree (2026-09-17):** other Claude sessions build and commit from `C:\src\JusPrin` and
`C:\src\JusPrin\build` concurrently. Do not patch that checkout or build there from a worktree session;
a link there holds `.lib` files and breaks their build (LNK1104). Use a separate tree instead: configure
with `-DBUILD_TESTS=ON -DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF -DSLIC3R_MSVC_PDB=OFF -DDEP_BUILD_DIR=C:/src/JusPrin/deps/build`
at a short path such as `C:\b\wsh`, which is a full `libslic3r_gui` build of about 40 minutes. To symbolize a crash
without a debugger, relink with a `ForceImportAfterCppTargets` props file (Link `GenerateDebugInformation`/`GenerateMapFile`),
read the fault offset from the event log (Application, event 1000), and run
`llvm-symbolizer --obj=<exe> --relative-address <offset>` (the symbolizer ships in the MSVC bin dir).

- The in-app browser pane renders a `file://` page as a static snapshot and refuses `screenshot`.
  To look at a rendered page (e.g. a vitest `PREVIEW_OUT` page), serve the directory over a
  throwaway node http server on 127.0.0.1 and navigate to that instead.

**Commits can hang in the `entire` hook (2026-09-25):** `git commit` from an agent session in a worktree
never returned; `entire hooks git prepare-commit-msg <file> message` alone hangs too (60 s, no output,
stdin closed). `--no-verify` does not skip prepare-commit-msg, and hooks must not be bypassed anyway, so
stop after one timed attempt (`timeout 90 git commit ... < /dev/null`), kill the orphaned `entire`
process it leaves behind (`ps -W | grep entire`), and ask Kenneth. Other sessions' commits carry an
`Entire-Checkpoint` trailer, so the hook works somewhere; the cause was not found.

**Concurrent harness runs collide on WebView2 (2026-09-25):** every harness exe uses the same WebView2
profile, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\JusPrin2\EBWebView`. While another session's harness is running (e.g. a
long `--home-printers-live` fixture run), a second harness fails at once with
`shell_agent_page_handshake_complete FAIL`, and its app log shows `JusPrin agent page failed to load:
The group or resource is not in the correct state`. That is not a page or bundle problem. Check for
`shell_integration_harness.exe` in `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process`, don't kill another session's
process, and set `$env:WEBVIEW2_USER_DATA_FOLDER='C:\b\<tree>-webview'` for your own runs.

**Scripting on this box (2026-10-06):** there is no `python`/`py`; use node (`C:\Users\guitest\.local\node-v24.21.0-win-x64`). Bash heredocs and `node -e "..."` that contain backticks, `${...}` or backslashes get mangled by the shell; write the script to a file with the Write tool and run `node <file>`. The main checkout's build tree `C:\src\JusPrin\build` (VS generator, Release) is fine to build from a session that is working in the main checkout: `cmake --build C:\src\JusPrin\build --config Release --target <targets> -- -m` after `vcvars64.bat`; harness exes there read `resources\` from the source tree, so `npm run build` in `AgentUI` is enough to refresh the Agent page. A touched `Workspace.hpp` rebuild of `libslic3r_gui` + `shell_integration_harness` takes roughly 10 minutes.

name: prompt-evals-on-deepseek-only
description: "Evaluate printer-panel prompt changes on DeepSeek V4 Flash (pinned OpenRouter hosts) only; don't add or report the app's gpt-5.4-mini alongside"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 8ce79576-0bc2-4fb6-be25-2d69c0fd25d2
  modified: 2026-10-13T05:49:02.816Z
---

Kenneth decided (2026-09-28) that prompt changes are evaluated on DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, pinned to hosts that answer the app's developer notes (`tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py` defaults), and on no other model. I had kept running and reporting the app's own gpt-5.4-mini next to it on every change; he asked why I treated the app's model as special, and had me remove the `--app` option and every "also check the app's model" instruction.

**Why:** it doubled cost and numbers to read, made the app's model look like a second judge, and JusPrin will soon support other providers, so today's default model isn't what users will necessarily get.

On 2026-10-13 Kenneth applied the same rule to the project assistant's journeys (`shell_integration_harness --journey`, `tests/project_journey/`): DeepSeek on OpenRouter with its hosted tool search, not the app's gpt-5.4-mini, even though the app's namespace deferral exists only on the OpenAI route. He put the keys on the Windows box that day at `C:\Users\guitest\.config\jusprin\prompt-test.env` (`export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=`, `export OPENAI_API_KEY=`); read them from there, never print them. He still approves the run count and token estimate before each live batch.

**How to apply:** judge and report prompt edits with the harness defaults only (paired `--prompt-rev HEAD` run). Use `--model` only when he asks to compare models. The real-app check (`shell_harness --printer-live`) still uses whatever the app is configured with; that's an app check, not a prompt evaluation. See [[fix-without-breaking-other-scenarios]].

name: entire-commit-hook-hangs
description: "git commit hangs in Entire's prepare-commit-msg on Windows because Entire opens CONIN$ for a [Y/n] link prompt; GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 makes it non-interactive"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 673eb384-7139-489f-8ef7-aa76f6ab7efa
  modified: 2026-09-27T05:53:11.186Z
---

Root cause (diagnosed 2026-09-25, Entire CLI 0.11.0): when the committing session has file changes to link,
`entire hooks git prepare-commit-msg <file> message` shows "Link this commit to session context? [Y/n]" and reads the
answer from `CONIN$`, not stdin. The agent's Git Bash has a hidden console, so the open succeeds and the read blocks forever.
`</dev/null` does not help. Commits with nothing to link skip the prompt, which is why it looked intermittent.
The log is buffered, so `.entire/logs/entire.log` shows nothing until the process exits.
Evidence: handle dump of the hung process showed a `\Device\ConDrv` handle with a blocked synchronous read.
Entire's own Pi integration prefixes agent bash commands with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` for this exact reason.
With `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` the same hook finished in ~0.3s and added the trailer, 3 of 3 runs; without it, 3 of 3 hung.

**Why:** It looks like a slow checkpoint condense, so it is easy to wait a long time for nothing.
A separate, real slowdown also exists: an `msbuild -m` build pins all 16 cores (processor queue ~64) and every
`entire` launch then takes 5-20s. That is slow, not hung; don't confuse the two.

**How to apply:** Fixed 2026-09-25: `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` is set as a user env var (HKCU\Environment), so Claude and Codex
shells inherit it after the app restarts (verified in Claude: 3/3 hook runs 0.3s with trailer). If a commit hangs again, first check
`echo $GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT` in the agent shell. Restarting the Claude app: the tray has no Quit, so end all `claude` processes
from a helper launched via WMI (outside Claude's tree) and relaunch with `explorer.exe shell:AppsFolder\Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc!Claude`.
If one hangs anyway, kill only that commit's `entire` PID; never `--no-verify`. See [[windows-build-machine]].

2026-09-27: with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` already set, a `git merge --no-ff` (merge commit) in a worktree still ran past a
120 s `timeout` -- but the merge commit was already written correctly and nothing was left running. After a timeout, check
`git log -1` and the parents before retrying; a retry would make a second commit. A plain `git commit` minutes earlier took ~seconds.
---
name: fix-without-breaking-other-scenarios
description: "Kenneth's standing concern: I over-focus on the problem in front of me and my fix breaks situations not in view; measure the whole scenario set before and after"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 50d5527e-64d5-4a8c-a3c1-5370fb831020
  modified: 2026-09-28T18:48:29.778Z
---

When fixing one visible failure (e.g. a system-prompt bug in one conversation mode), Kenneth expects the fix to be judged against every related scenario, not just the reported one. He said (2026-09-28) that I tend to solve the problem in front of me and break "a lot more situations" that aren't in view, and asked me to research best practice online instead of reasoning from the one bug.

**Why:** On the printer-panel prompt this was borne out: a two-line fix for the Change conversation silently took Add-mode `add-not-now-done` from 19/20 to 3/20; only a side-by-side full-suite run caught it.

**How to apply:**
- Before editing a shared prompt/component, build or extend a test set covering all its scenarios (off-script inputs, regressions from git history), then compare old vs new in the same run (`tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --prompt-rev HEAD`).
- Scope a fix to the scenario it's for; keep measured wording for the others byte-identical.
- Don't let the current bug drive general recommendations — look for external best practice first.
---
name: write-reports-in-plain-english
description: "Kenneth finds dense, jargon-heavy status reports very hard to read; restate in plain English with common-sense reasoning, not tables of counts"
metadata:

  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 71e3bd46-c856-4b36-b7cc-979fe94e0bdf

Root cause (diagnosed 2026-09-25, Entire CLI 0.11.0): when the committing session has file changes to link,
`entire hooks git prepare-commit-msg <file> message` shows "Link this commit to session context? [Y/n]" and reads the
answer from `CONIN$`, not stdin. The agent's Git Bash has a hidden console, so the open succeeds and the read blocks forever.
`</dev/null` does not help. Commits with nothing to link skip the prompt, which is why it looked intermittent.
The log is buffered, so `.entire/logs/entire.log` shows nothing until the process exits.
Evidence: handle dump of the hung process showed a `\Device\ConDrv` handle with a blocked synchronous read.
Entire's own Pi integration prefixes agent bash commands with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` for this exact reason.
With `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` the same hook finished in ~0.3s and added the trailer, 3 of 3 runs; without it, 3 of 3 hung.

**Why:** It looks like a slow checkpoint condense, so it is easy to wait a long time for nothing.
A separate, real slowdown also exists: an `msbuild -m` build pins all 16 cores (processor queue ~64) and every
`entire` launch then takes 5-20s. That is slow, not hung; don't confuse the two.

**How to apply:** Fixed 2026-09-25: `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` is set as a user env var (HKCU\Environment), so Claude and Codex
shells inherit it after the app restarts (verified in Claude: 3/3 hook runs 0.3s with trailer). If a commit hangs again, first check
`echo $GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT` in the agent shell. Restarting the Claude app: the tray has no Quit, so end all `claude` processes
from a helper launched via WMI (outside Claude's tree) and relaunch with `explorer.exe shell:AppsFolder\Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc!Claude`.
If one hangs anyway, kill only that commit's `entire` PID; never `--no-verify`. See [[windows-build-machine]].

2026-09-27: with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` already set, a `git merge --no-ff` (merge commit) in a worktree still ran past a
120 s `timeout` -- but the merge commit was already written correctly and nothing was left running. After a timeout, check
`git log -1` and the parents before retrying; a retry would make a second commit. A plain `git commit` minutes earlier took ~seconds.

content.content:
**1. `defer_loading` and what the model sees**

- The guide says that for namespaces, "`defer_loading` applies to the functions inside the namespace, not to the namespace object itself."
- For a namespace or MCP server, the model initially sees only the container's name and description, not the functions inside it.
- For an individual deferred function, the model still sees its name and description. Tool search mainly defers the parameter schema.
- Tools without `defer_loading: true` are callable right away.

**2. Calling a deferred tool that hasn't been loaded**

The guide doesn't explicitly say whether such a call is refused or auto-loaded. It implies the tool is unavailable: "Tools that were not listed as part of this array will not be available to the model." Loading happens through tool search, not automatically on call.

**3. Persistence across turns and stateless use**

- For client-executed search, the guide says loaded tools persist: "The model will be able to call any of these tools in future turns," so you don't need to reload them.
- Changing the loaded set has a cost: "changing the loaded tool set will break the model's cache from that point forward."
- The guide doesn't address `store=false` or stateless operation. Its examples show two ways to continue a conversation. The JavaScript and Python examples resend the first response's output items followed by the `tool_search_output`. The Go, Java, and Ruby examples use `previous_response_id`.
- For client mode, the `tool_search_output` must echo the same `call_id` from the `tool_search_call`.
- For `additional_tools` items, the guide says to "preserve the item's position" when round-tripping conversation items manually, so the model sees the same tools at the same point.
- Hosted search output has `call_id: null`, so the `call_id` echo rule applies only to client mode.

**4. Recommendations on how many tools to keep loaded**

- The only explicit number is for namespace size: "aim to keep each namespace to fewer than 10 functions for better token efficiency and model performance."
- The guide doesn't give a recommended number of loaded tools at any one time.
- It recommends deferred loading for "a large catalog where each task needs only a few functions," and eager loading for "a small set of functions, or functions needed for most tasks."
- Mixing eager and deferred functions in Agents API sessions is "generally not recommended."
- It suggests comparing task completion, input-token usage, and latency on representative requests before choosing a default.

**5. Request format**

**1. `defer_loading` on functions**

Setting `defer_loading: true` on a function withholds it. The guide says, "Deferred tools are hidden by default: the model cannot see or call one until a search returns it." It doesn't explicitly say whether a deferred tool's name or description appears anywhere before a search, but the "hidden" wording implies the model sees nothing until then.

**2. Calling a deferred tool that hasn't been loaded**

The guide doesn't describe this case directly. It says the model "cannot see or call" a deferred tool until a search returns it, so a direct call should not be possible. It does not say whether such a call is refused with an error or handled some other way. Nothing in the guide suggests deferred tools are auto-loaded.

**3. Persistence across turns and carrying state**

Discovered tools persist. "Discovering a tool does not disturb the tools already in the conversation," and prompt caching is preserved across searches. The guide also says "Each turn records only what changed, such as the ID of a tool it loaded," so loaded tools are tracked from turn to turn.

To carry this forward, return assistant messages unchanged: "Send assistant messages back exactly as returned, including the encrypted reasoning described above." On the Responses API, the state sits in a reasoning item's `encrypted_content`. The guide does not describe separate tool-search items. Also, keep `tools`, `tool_choice`, and `deferred_tools` identical on every turn, and don't edit, remove, or reorder earlier messages.

**4. How many tools to keep loaded**

The guide recommends: "Keep your three to five most frequently used tools loaded." Tools the model needs on almost every request should stay loaded, because deferring them costs more in search round-trips than it saves in tokens. For context, standard tool calling is a better fit "below about 10 tools."

**5. Responses API request format and namespaces**

- Add `{ "type": "openrouter:tool_search" }` to the `tools` array. The alias `tool_search` is also accepted on Responses.
- Mark each withheld function with `"defer_loading": true`. The example shows `name`, `description`, and `parameters` alongside it.
- `openrouter:tool_search` itself cannot be deferred; doing so returns a `400`.
- If you set `tool_choice`, it must be `{"type": "allowed_tools", ...}` or omitted. On Responses, `allowed_tools` is authoritative: a deferred tool left out of it is revoked and can't be found by search.

The Quick Start example uses a `messages` field, which is Chat Completions style, even though the guide says Chat Completions rejects the tool type. The guide doesn't resolve this, so check it against the Responses API reference.

Namespaces are not mentioned. The only related term is naming prefixes (for example, `github_issues_list`), which help search but are not namespaces. The guide gives no evidence that namespaces are supported.
