content.content:
## Tool budget and tool shape

The limit on the number of tools comes from how much the model has to load on each turn. It does not come from how much the app can do. The rules in this section rest on this evidence:

- OpenAI's function-calling guidance keeps fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn and defers the rest.
- Anthropic's [tool-writing guidance](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) asks for a few tools aimed at high-impact workflows. It names "tools that merely wrap existing software functionality or API endpoints" as the common error.
- A [domain-oriented MCP study](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.22063v1) measured three interfaces. A generic interface of thin tools scored below raw SQL. Tools shaped around the domain scored far above both.
- The "god tool", one tool that dispatches many unrelated actions through a single `action` parameter, is a documented anti-pattern.

The current five-tool MCP catalog measures about 1.9 KB per definition, and two thirds of that is output schema.

**How tools are loaded.** Tool search is a capability of the configured provider and model. We declare it in configuration. The code never guesses it from a model name or an endpoint URL. `OpenAIResponsesConfig::tool_search` takes one of three values:

- `None` gives the model the full catalog from the start, as ordinary function calling. It is also how to turn deferral off.
- `Functions` turns on hosted search over functions that are deferred one by one.
- `Namespaces` turns on hosted search over deferred toolsets.

Deferral is on by default for the route the app ships with. When nothing is declared, `resolve_tool_search` gives the built-in model on the built-in endpoint `Namespaces`. That pair was checked live (see Deferral below). A different model or a different endpoint gets `None` until its own capability is declared, because nothing has been checked for it.

Any model on any compatible endpoint can use any mode it supports, without a code change. For a model or endpoint other than the built-in pair, declaring no capability keeps ordinary function calling. It does not make the model unavailable. When deferral is on, three reads stay loaded from the start: `workspace_inspect`, `settings_search`, and `settings_get`. This is a starting policy. It is not a measured ranking of how often each tool is called. Printer and filament sessions keep their small catalogs fully loaded. MCP is unchanged, because MCP clients do their own deferral.

The app reads `tool_search` from the `jusprin_agent` section of AppConfig. The value is `none`, `functions`, or `namespaces`. The environment variable `JUSPRIN_AGENT_TOOL_SEARCH` overrides it. An empty value means the default for the route. An invalid value is a configuration error. Keep this setting with the model and endpoint settings, and update it when you change provider. There is no allowlist of models or endpoints. The app does not probe the provider at run time, and it does not retry a request with a rewritten catalog. This capability only selects the shape of the Responses request. Support for a different API protocol still belongs in that provider's adapter.

Every request still sends the complete catalog, in the same order. That includes `object_import` even when there is no attachment. Running an import without an importable attachment is still refused. A search never rewrites the `tools` array, so the bytes sent do not shrink. What is saved is the definitions that the provider holds back from the model's context at the start. The input tokens and cached tokens that the provider reports remain the authority on actual usage. The budget is 20 definitions per turn. Going over 20 does not block anything. It is the point at which we start watching the measurements.

**The baseline, measured on Windows against the live app.**

| After milestone | In-app definitions | In-app bytes | MCP definitions | MCP bytes | MCP bytes through the offline helper recipe |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| M0 | 7 | 3,145 | 5 | 3,147 | |
| M1 | 11 | 6,482 | 9 | 6,915 | |
| M2 | 18 | 12,721 | 16 | 13,911 | 13,894 |
| M3 | 20 | 19,331 | 21 | 22,661 | 22,639 |
| M4 | 20 | 21,594 | 21 | 24,923 | 24,901 |
| M5 | 25 | 29,148 | 26 | 33,013 | |

The M5 figure for MCP was read over two `tools/list` pages.

The `--live-agent` regression test, run at M0 and at M1, shows what those definitions cost in tokens. The first request of a conversation gets nothing from the cache and pays for the whole catalog: 803 tokens at M0 and 1,733 at M1. So four more definitions cost about 930 tokens, paid once. Every later request in the same conversation came back 77 to 92 per cent cached (at M1, 5,864 input tokens, of which 5,376 were cached). That is because the tools array is byte-identical through a chat, and the cache depends on that. At M2, the same test made eleven requests that took 2,875 to 6,763 input tokens, with 42 to 91 per cent cached. None of the eleven started with an empty cache, because an earlier run on the same day had already cached the shared beginning of the prompt. So that run did not measure the uncached cost at M2.

Those cache hits are history. They lower the billed input cost. They do not remove definitions from the model's context, and they do not guarantee a hit on another request. The current catalog is over the 20-definition budget. Deferral targets the catalog's cost in the initial context while keeping the catalog stable. The live check under Deferral below gives the first figures for actual usage. Selection accuracy and latency across real tasks still need an approved live comparison.

**The printer panel follows the same rule with its own set of tools.** The printer panel on Home runs its own conversation, `PrinterConversation`. That conversation is offered the five printer tools and the four settings tools. The list is the same in every mode (Add, Change, or Connect), so it stays byte-identical through a conversation and between conversations of the same mode.

What a call may do depends on the conversation. `PrinterConversation::preflight_tool` refuses every call that is not allowed, before any card is shown, with an error that says where to go instead. The rules are:

- Finding and adding a printer (`printer_identify`, `printer_add`) is allowed only in an Add conversation. A Change or Connect conversation is about a printer the person already has. An add there would save another printer and move the conversation onto it.
- `printer_change` is allowed only on the printer the conversation is about, once there is one.
- The connection tools are allowed only once there is a saved printer.
- The settings tools are allowed only with `scope: "printer"`, on the printer the conversation is about.

A Change conversation may be about a stock profile (one that ships with OrcaSlicer) that the project has selected. That happens when the person chooses Printer settings… in the header on a project that uses a stock profile. In that case, changes to the nozzle and to the connection are refused with `stock_profile`. Changes to settings are saved as a copy of the profile, and the conversation follows that copy from then on (`PrinterConversation::tool_settled`). A Change conversation is never turned into an Add conversation. The code that opens a Change conversation checks that the printer is there, and shows OrcaSlicer's error dialog when it is not.

The header's filament chat uses the same panel (`PrinterPanel::open_filament`). It is offered the four settings tools and nothing else, and it gets no project state. It has its own instructions. The page writes them in `AgentUI/src/filamentInstructions.ts` and sends them with `filament_instructions`. The page writes them from the facts the app sends as the session part of the panel's state (`PrinterPanel::filament_session_json`): the preset's name, its slot and material, and, for a stock filament, the copy that a change is saved as. The preflight check for this chat allows the settings tools only with `scope: "filament"` on that preset. It refuses an apply that has no `persistAs`, with `not_saved`, because the chat is gone when it closes. When a copy is saved in the preset's place, the chat is about that copy from then on, and the page writes the instructions again for the copy. Until 2026-09-29 the filament chat ran on the project assistant's instructions and tools. With those, the model read "make the nozzle 5 degrees hotter" as a request to print. In another run it set 205 °C when the value was 220 °C, without reading the value first.

We do not give each mode a different tool list, for two reasons. The conversation has to refuse disallowed calls anyway, whatever list the model is shown. And the way to restrict tools while keeping the list stable (`tool_choice` with `allowed_tools`) exists only on some providers. We would reconsider if transcripts showed the model reaching for a refused tool and then failing to recover. `tests/printer_prompt` measures this with the `change-add-another` case.

Two past changes explain the current design:

- Until 2026-09-23 the panel offered one tool per mode (7f66e75b07). The reason was to keep a printer lookup from clearing the pinned card of the printer a Change session was about. That card is gone (4d4f9e466b). Offering one tool per step also left an Add conversation with no tool to connect the printer it had just added (8334b3395b).
- On 2026-09-28 three tools were removed (b60fc2d8e6): `printer_manual_setup`, `printer_manual_connection` and `printer_setup_finish`. These were the tools that opened a window or closed the panel. OrcaSlicer's full printer list and a printer's settings are still reachable from the panel's own buttons, and the person closes the panel.

The app decides which tools are offered. The page writes the text: `AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts` holds the instructions, and `AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts` holds the notes the model reads after a tap. If a turn arrives before the page has written its instructions, the app refuses the turn. It does not send the turn with the project assistant's prompt. The instructions for an Add conversation carry the whole printer list, about 28 KB. That text is always the same and sits at the start of the instructions, so it is cached. No printer conversation carries the project: no workspace state goes into the turn, and none goes into a tool result.

**Deferral.** Deferral means the model first sees only a short index and loads a tool's full definition when it needs it. Use the hosted mechanism that the model platform provides. Never write our own mechanism for switching tools in and out. We checked the documentation on 2026-10-10:

- [GPT-5.4 mini's model page](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.4-mini) lists tool search.
- [OpenAI's Responses guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-tool-search) documents `tool_search`, `defer_loading: true` on a single function, and namespace discovery. It also says that loaded definitions are appended at the end of the context, which preserves the cache.
- [OpenRouter's hosted tool search](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search) documents `tool_search` on the Responses API as an alias of `openrouter:tool_search`, with `defer_loading`, across models and providers. At the level of documentation, this covers the DeepSeek V4 Flash route that the prompt tests use. That documentation does not establish namespace discovery, so `functions` is the documented setting for this route. It also says that this hosted search does not support Chat Completions.

These are examples of configurations that the documentation supports. They are not a complete list of supported models or endpoints. Choose the capability from the provider's documentation. Do not infer it from the name of a model or a vendor.

With the `namespaces` capability, JusPrin advertises eight namespaces, and each has fewer than ten deferred functions. A deferred namespace shows its name and description at the start. A function that is deferred individually still shows its own name and description.

The provider's `tool_search_call` and `tool_search_output` items are kept exactly as received, next to the namespaced function calls, while a turn continues over stateless requests. They are not app tools and they never reach the coordinator. Across user turns, the app replays its own history of calls and results, and gives each function its current namespace. It does not keep the provider's search history, so a later turn may discover the same tool again. The tools array stays byte-identical. There is no tool that enables a toolset, no rewriting of schemas after discovery, and no change to the MCP server.

**The live check behind the default.** On 2026-10-12 the `--live-agent` scenario ran against `gpt-5.4-mini` on OpenAI's endpoint, once with the full catalog and twice with `namespaces` (once declared, once left to the default). Each run makes four requests: a question answered from context, a request to copy an object with `plate_layout`, the continuation after that tool call, and a later user turn. All three runs passed every check.

| Request | Full catalog, input tokens | `namespaces`, input tokens |
|---|---:|---:|
| First request, nothing cached | 7,115 | 2,175 |
| Request that calls `plate_layout` | 7,141 | 3,377 |
| Continuation after the tool call | 7,683 | 3,919 |
| Later user turn | 7,418 | 2,475 |
| Total | 29,357 | 11,946 |

What the runs show:

- OpenAI accepts the request shape: namespaces, `tool_search`, and `defer_loading`, with `store: false`.
- The model found a deferred tool. Its response held a `tool_search_call`, a `tool_search_output`, and then a `function_call` to `plate_layout` in the `geometry` namespace. The search and the call came back in one response, so there was no extra request.
- The continuation that passes the search items back was accepted. So was the later user turn, which replays the namespaced call from the app's own history without the search items.
- The first request was 4,940 tokens smaller. The estimate from bytes, at four bytes per token, was about 7,191. Trust the provider's count, not the estimate.
- Later requests were still served partly from the cache (1,792 to 3,328 cached tokens with `namespaces`).

What they do not show: this is one short scenario with one tool call, run once or twice. It says nothing yet about how often the model picks the right tool across real tasks, about latency, or about any other model or provider. `functions` mode and OpenRouter have not been run live at all.

The native tests use a fake transport. They verify the shape of the request, that schemas are preserved, replay, and that the catalog is stable. They do not verify that a provider accepts the request or that the model selects the right tool. The offline test commands do not authorize any live request. Before any live batch, Kenneth must approve the number of runs and the token estimate. Log `usage` on every response and report the total, including judge requests and continuations.

**Shape each tool as a domain operation.** A tool does one thing that a slicer user has a name for: place an object, lay out the plates, mark a region, set up the printer. Do not wrap each OrcaSlicer function in its own tool. Do not build a tool that interprets a list of unrelated commands. One operation may have several optional facets, as long as each facet has its own type and the tool rejects facets that conflict.

**Batch only where items share a shape.** Good examples are a list of setting changes, a list of intent fields, a list of annotations, and a list of layout rows with one row per object. A list that mixes transforms, imports, and deletes is the god tool described above. It is refused.

**Fold reads into sections and detail levels before adding a read tool.** A new read tool is justified in only two cases. Either its inputs are of a different kind (a search over a large catalog, an analysis of one object, a report on a sliced plate), or its result is an image.

**Let call logs decide consolidation.** If transcripts show that two tools are always called together, consider merging them. If two facets of one tool are never used together, consider splitting them. Make these decisions from eval evidence, not from a design discussion.

**Output schemas are not advertised over MCP.** No client was shown to use them, and they were two thirds of the catalog. `tools/list` no longer carries `outputSchema`. `validate_output` still checks every successful MCP result, so a result that breaks its contract still fails with a visible error. We measured the effect on one build, with the recipe near the end of this guide. With five tools, the catalog went from 9,723 bytes to 3,141, which is from about 2,430 tokens to 785. Only the MCP side saves anything. The in-app adapter has always sent `input_schema` as `parameters` and nothing else, so an in-app turn never carried output schemas. Restore the field only for a client that is shown to read it.

=== catalog toolsets ===
### Toolsets and loading

| Toolset | Tools | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `core` | 10 | Every turn: state, geometry facts, settings, intent, plan, slicing. |
| `project` | 2 | Opening, reading attachments. |
| `setup` | 4 | Choosing or confirming printer, plate, filament, process preset. |
| `geometry` | 5 | Placing, laying out, importing, deleting. |
| `reshape` | 4 | Cutting, splitting, merging, repairing. |
| `regions` | 1 | Marking local meaning. |
| `check` | 3 | Inspecting a sliced result beyond the report. |
| `output` | 3 | Preflight, send, export. |
| `machine` | 3 | Other printers, camera, pause and stop. |
| `calibration` | 2 | Calibration tests. |

MCP still lists its whole catalog. A project conversation that is configured for deferral keeps three reads loaded and defers the implemented groups below. Each size is the sum of the compact UTF-8 JSON of the group's functions, before array separators.

| Toolset | Deferred functions | Full bytes |
|---|---|---:|
| `core` | `object_analyze`, `settings_preview_patch`, `settings_apply_patch`, `intent_update`, `plan_set`, `slice_start`, `slice_report` | 10,112 |
| `project` | `project_open`, `project_attachment_read` | 1,922 |
| `setup` | `presets_list`, `printer_list`, `printer_setup_preview`, `printer_setup` | 3,200 |
| `geometry` | `object_place`, `plate_layout`, `object_import`, `project_delete_items` | 5,456 |
| `reshape` | `object_divide_preview`, `object_divide`, `object_merge`, `object_repair` | 3,189 |
| `regions` | `region_annotate` | 2,759 |
| `check` | `view_render`, `slice_inspect`, `activity_cancel` | 2,045 |
| `output` | `export_file` | 1,162 |

`machine` and `calibration` have no implemented project functions yet. The three reads that stay loaded keep their full canonical schemas. Together they are 4,040 bytes before separators.

These figures were measured offline on 2026-10-12 from the registry. Before import was always advertised, the catalog without an attachment was 28 functions and 33,058 bytes. The stable full catalog is 29 functions and 33,915 bytes, because import is now always advertised. With `namespaces`, the catalog on the wire is 35,648 bytes. Its projection into the initial context is 5,151 bytes. That is 28,764 bytes less than the full stable catalog (85%, about 7,191 tokens at four bytes per token). Against the earlier catalog without an attachment, the reduction is 27,907 bytes (about 6,977 tokens).

The native `[budget]` test computes that projection from the registry: the loaded functions, the namespace names and descriptions, and the tool search entry. A conservative projection for OpenRouter keeps the name and description of every deferred function. It is 20,503 bytes, a reduction of 13,412 bytes (about 3,353 tokens). OpenRouter's documentation says deferred tools are hidden entirely, so what the model actually sees and how tokens are counted may differ. All of these figures estimate the initial context. They are not counts from a model's tokenizer, and they are not billed savings per request. Discovered schemas, search steps, history, and the provider's own serialization can add tokens later.

Any model on any compatible endpoint can use any mode it supports, without a code change. For a model or endpoint other than the built-in pair, declaring no capability keeps ordinary function calling. It does not make the model unavailable. When deferral is on, three reads stay loaded from the start: `workspace_inspect`, `settings_search`, and `settings_get`. This is a starting policy. It is not a measured ranking of how often each tool is called. Printer and filament sessions keep their small catalogs fully loaded. MCP is unchanged, because MCP clients do their own deferral.

The app reads `tool_search` from the `jusprin_agent` section of AppConfig. The value is `none`, `functions`, or `namespaces`. The environment variable `JUSPRIN_AGENT_TOOL_SEARCH` overrides it. An empty value means the default for the route. An invalid value is a configuration error. Keep this setting with the model and endpoint settings, and update it when you change provider. There is no allowlist of models or endpoints. The app does not probe the provider at run time, and it does not retry a request with a rewritten catalog. This capability only selects the shape of the Responses request. Support for a different API protocol still belongs in that provider's adapter.

Every request still sends the complete catalog, in the same order. That includes `object_import` even when there is no attachment. Running an import without an importable attachment is still refused. A search never rewrites the `tools` array, so the bytes sent do not shrink. What is saved is the definitions that the provider holds back from the model's context at the start. The input tokens and cached tokens that the provider reports remain the authority on actual usage. The budget is 20 definitions per turn. Going over 20 does not block anything. It is the point at which we start watching the measurements.

**The baseline, measured on Windows against the live app.**

| After milestone | In-app definitions | In-app bytes | MCP definitions | MCP bytes | MCP bytes through the offline helper recipe |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| M0 | 7 | 3,145 | 5 | 3,147 | |
| M1 | 11 | 6,482 | 9 | 6,915 | |
| M2 | 18 | 12,721 | 16 | 13,911 | 13,894 |
| M3 | 20 | 19,331 | 21 | 22,661 | 22,639 |
| M4 | 20 | 21,594 | 21 | 24,923 | 24,901 |
| M5 | 25 | 29,148 | 26 | 33,013 | |

The M5 figure for MCP was read over two `tools/list` pages.

The `--live-agent` regression test, run at M0 and at M1, shows what those definitions cost in tokens. The first request of a conversation gets nothing from the cache and pays for the whole catalog: 803 tokens at M0 and 1,733 at M1. So four more definitions cost about 930 tokens, paid once. Every later request in the same conversation came back 77 to 92 per cent cached (at M1, 5,864 input tokens, of which 5,376 were cached). That is because the tools array is byte-identical through a chat, and the cache depends on that. At M2, the same test made eleven requests that took 2,875 to 6,763 input tokens, with 42 to 91 per cent cached. None of the eleven started with an empty cache, because an earlier run on the same day had already cached the shared beginning of the prompt. So that run did not measure the uncached cost at M2.

Those cache hits are history. They lower the billed input cost. They do not remove definitions from the model's context, and they do not guarantee a hit on another request. The current catalog is over the 20-definition budget. Deferral targets the catalog's cost in the initial context while keeping the catalog stable. The live check under Deferral below gives the first figures for actual usage. Selection accuracy and latency across real tasks still need an approved live comparison.

**The printer panel follows the same rule with its own set of tools.** The printer panel on Home runs its own conversation, `PrinterConversation`. That conversation is offered the five printer tools and the four settings tools. The list is the same in every mode (Add, Change, or Connect), so it stays byte-identical through a conversation and between conversations of the same mode.

What a call may do depends on the conversation. `PrinterConversation::preflight_tool` refuses every call that is not allowed, before any card is shown, with an error that says where to go instead. The rules are:

- Finding and adding a printer (`printer_identify`, `printer_add`) is allowed only in an Add conversation. A Change or Connect conversation is about a printer the person already has. An add there would save another printer and move the conversation onto it.
- `printer_change` is allowed only on the printer the conversation is about, once there is one.
- The connection tools are allowed only once there is a saved printer.
- The settings tools are allowed only with `scope: "printer"`, on the printer the conversation is about.

A Change conversation may be about a stock profile (one that ships with OrcaSlicer) that the project has selected. That happens when the person chooses Printer settings… in the header on a project that uses a stock profile. In that case, changes to the nozzle and to the connection are refused with `stock_profile`. Changes to settings are saved as a copy of the profile, and the conversation follows that copy from then on (`PrinterConversation::tool_settled`). A Change conversation is never turned into an Add conversation. The code that opens a Change conversation checks that the printer is there, and shows OrcaSlicer's error dialog when it is not.

The header's filament chat uses the same panel (`PrinterPanel::open_filament`). It is offered the four settings tools and nothing else, and it gets no project state. It has its own instructions. The page writes them in `AgentUI/src/filamentInstructions.ts` and sends them with `filament_instructions`. The page writes them from the facts the app sends as the session part of the panel's state (`PrinterPanel::filament_session_json`): the preset's name, its slot and material, and, for a stock filament, the copy that a change is saved as. The preflight check for this chat allows the settings tools only with `scope: "filament"` on that preset. It refuses an apply that has no `persistAs`, with `not_saved`, because the chat is gone when it closes. When a copy is saved in the preset's place, the chat is about that copy from then on, and the page writes the instructions again for the copy. Until 2026-09-29 the filament chat ran on the project assistant's instructions and tools. With those, the model read "make the nozzle 5 degrees hotter" as a request to print. In another run it set 205 °C when the value was 220 °C, without reading the value first.

We do not give each mode a different tool list, for two reasons. The conversation has to refuse disallowed calls anyway, whatever list the model is shown. And the way to restrict tools while keeping the list stable (`tool_choice` with `allowed_tools`) exists only on some providers. We would reconsider if transcripts showed the model reaching for a refused tool and then failing to recover. `tests/printer_prompt` measures this with the `change-add-another` case.

Two past changes explain the current design:

- Until 2026-09-23 the panel offered one tool per mode (7f66e75b07). The reason was to keep a printer lookup from clearing the pinned card of the printer a Change session was about. That card is gone (4d4f9e466b). Offering one tool per step also left an Add conversation with no tool to connect the printer it had just added (8334b3395b).
- On 2026-09-28 three tools were removed (b60fc2d8e6): `printer_manual_setup`, `printer_manual_connection` and `printer_setup_finish`. These were the tools that opened a window or closed the panel. OrcaSlicer's full printer list and a printer's settings are still reachable from the panel's own buttons, and the person closes the panel.

The app decides which tools are offered. The page writes the text: `AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts` holds the instructions, and `AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts` holds the notes the model reads after a tap. If a turn arrives before the page has written its instructions, the app refuses the turn. It does not send the turn with the project assistant's prompt. The instructions for an Add conversation carry the whole printer list, about 28 KB. That text is always the same and sits at the start of the instructions, so it is cached. No printer conversation carries the project: no workspace state goes into the turn, and none goes into a tool result.

**Deferral.** Deferral means the model first sees only a short index and loads a tool's full definition when it needs it. Use the hosted mechanism that the model platform provides. Never write our own mechanism for switching tools in and out. We checked the documentation on 2026-10-10:

- [GPT-5.4 mini's model page](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.4-mini) lists tool search.
- [OpenAI's Responses guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-tool-search) documents `tool_search`, `defer_loading: true` on a single function, and namespace discovery. It also says that loaded definitions are appended at the end of the context, which preserves the cache.
- [OpenRouter's hosted tool search](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/tool-search) documents `tool_search` on the Responses API as an alias of `openrouter:tool_search`, with `defer_loading`, across models and providers. At the level of documentation, this covers the DeepSeek V4 Flash route that the prompt tests use. That documentation does not establish namespace discovery, so `functions` is the documented setting for this route. It also says that this hosted search does not support Chat Completions.

These are examples of configurations that the documentation supports. They are not a complete list of supported models or endpoints. Choose the capability from the provider's documentation. Do not infer it from the name of a model or a vendor.

With the `namespaces` capability, JusPrin advertises eight namespaces, and each has fewer than ten deferred functions. A deferred namespace shows its name and description at the start. A function that is deferred individually still shows its own name and description.

The provider's `tool_search_call` and `tool_search_output` items are kept exactly as received, next to the namespaced function calls, while a turn continues over stateless requests. They are not app tools and they never reach the coordinator. Across user turns, the app replays its own history of calls and results, and gives each function its current namespace. It does not keep the provider's search history, so a later turn may discover the same tool again. The tools array stays byte-identical. There is no tool that enables a toolset, no rewriting of schemas after discovery, and no change to the MCP server.

**The live check behind the default.** On 2026-10-12 the `--live-agent` scenario ran against `gpt-5.4-mini` on OpenAI's endpoint, once with the full catalog and twice with `namespaces` (once declared, once left to the default). Each run makes four requests: a question answered from context, a request to copy an object with `plate_layout`, the continuation after that tool call, and a later user turn. All three runs passed every check.

| Request | Full catalog, input tokens | `namespaces`, input tokens |
|---|---:|---:|
| First request, nothing cached | 7,115 | 2,175 |
| Request that calls `plate_layout` | 7,141 | 3,377 |
| Continuation after the tool call | 7,683 | 3,919 |
| Later user turn | 7,418 | 2,475 |
| Total | 29,357 | 11,946 |

What the runs show:

- OpenAI accepts the request shape: namespaces, `tool_search`, and `defer_loading`, with `store: false`.
- The model found a deferred tool. Its response held a `tool_search_call`, a `tool_search_output`, and then a `function_call` to `plate_layout` in the `geometry` namespace. The search and the call came back in one response, so there was no extra request.
- The continuation that passes the search items back was accepted. So was the later user turn, which replays the namespaced call from the app's own history without the search items.
- The first request was 4,940 tokens smaller. The estimate from bytes, at four bytes per token, was about 7,191. Trust the provider's count, not the estimate.
- Later requests were still served partly from the cache (1,792 to 3,328 cached tokens with `namespaces`).

What they do not show: this is one short scenario with one tool call, run once or twice. It says nothing yet about how often the model picks the right tool across real tasks, about latency, or about any other model or provider. `functions` mode and OpenRouter have not been run live at all.

The native tests use a fake transport. They verify the shape of the request, that schemas are preserved, replay, and that the catalog is stable. They do not verify that a provider accepts the request or that the model selects the right tool. The offline test commands do not authorize any live request. Before any live batch, Kenneth must approve the number of runs and the token estimate. Log `usage` on every response and report the total, including judge requests and continuations.

**Shape each tool as a domain operation.** A tool does one thing that a slicer user has a name for: place an object, lay out the plates, mark a region, set up the printer. Do not wrap each OrcaSlicer function in its own tool. Do not build a tool that interprets a list of unrelated commands. One operation may have several optional facets, as long as each facet has its own type and the tool rejects facets that conflict.

**Batch only where items share a shape.** Good examples are a list of setting changes, a list of intent fields, a list of annotations, and a list of layout rows with one row per object. A list that mixes transforms, imports, and deletes is the god tool described above. It is refused.

**Fold reads into sections and detail levels before adding a read tool.** A new read tool is justified in only two cases. Either its inputs are of a different kind (a search over a large catalog, an analysis of one object, a report on a sliced plate), or its result is an image.

**Let call logs decide consolidation.** If transcripts show that two tools are always called together, consider merging them. If two facets of one tool are never used together, consider splitting them. Make these decisions from eval evidence, not from a design discussion.

**Output schemas are not advertised over MCP.** No client was shown to use them, and they were two thirds of the catalog. `tools/list` no longer carries `outputSchema`. `validate_output` still checks every successful MCP result, so a result that breaks its contract still fails with a visible error. We measured the effect on one build, with the recipe near the end of this guide. With five tools, the catalog went from 9,723 bytes to 3,141, which is from about 2,430 tokens to 785. Only the MCP side saves anything. The in-app adapter has always sent `input_schema` as `parameters` and nothing else, so an in-app turn never carried output schemas. Restore the field only for a client that is shown to read it.

=== catalog toolsets ===
### Toolsets and loading

| Toolset | Tools | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `core` | 10 | Every turn: state, geometry facts, settings, intent, plan, slicing. |
| `project` | 2 | Opening, reading attachments. |
| `setup` | 4 | Choosing or confirming printer, plate, filament, process preset. |
| `geometry` | 5 | Placing, laying out, importing, deleting. |
| `reshape` | 4 | Cutting, splitting, merging, repairing. |
| `regions` | 1 | Marking local meaning. |
| `check` | 3 | Inspecting a sliced result beyond the report. |
| `output` | 3 | Preflight, send, export. |
| `machine` | 3 | Other printers, camera, pause and stop. |
| `calibration` | 2 | Calibration tests. |

MCP still lists its whole catalog. A project conversation that is configured for deferral keeps three reads loaded and defers the implemented groups below. Each size is the sum of the compact UTF-8 JSON of the group's functions, before array separators.

| Toolset | Deferred functions | Full bytes |
|---|---|---:|
| `core` | `object_analyze`, `settings_preview_patch`, `settings_apply_patch`, `intent_update`, `plan_set`, `slice_start`, `slice_report` | 10,112 |
| `project` | `project_open`, `project_attachment_read` | 1,922 |
| `setup` | `presets_list`, `printer_list`, `printer_setup_preview`, `printer_setup` | 3,200 |
| `geometry` | `object_place`, `plate_layout`, `object_import`, `project_delete_items` | 5,456 |
| `reshape` | `object_divide_preview`, `object_divide`, `object_merge`, `object_repair` | 3,189 |
| `regions` | `region_annotate` | 2,759 |
| `check` | `view_render`, `slice_inspect`, `activity_cancel` | 2,045 |
| `output` | `export_file` | 1,162 |

`machine` and `calibration` have no implemented project functions yet. The three reads that stay loaded keep their full canonical schemas. Together they are 4,040 bytes before separators.

These figures were measured offline on 2026-10-12 from the registry. Before import was always advertised, the catalog without an attachment was 28 functions and 33,058 bytes. The stable full catalog is 29 functions and 33,915 bytes, because import is now always advertised. With `namespaces`, the catalog on the wire is 35,648 bytes. Its projection into the initial context is 5,151 bytes. That is 28,764 bytes less than the full stable catalog (85%, about 7,191 tokens at four bytes per token). Against the earlier catalog without an attachment, the reduction is 27,907 bytes (about 6,977 tokens).

The native `[budget]` test computes that projection from the registry: the loaded functions, the namespace names and descriptions, and the tool search entry. A conservative projection for OpenRouter keeps the name and description of every deferred function. It is 20,503 bytes, a reduction of 13,412 bytes (about 3,353 tokens). OpenRouter's documentation says deferred tools are hidden entirely, so what the model actually sees and how tokens are counted may differ. All of these figures estimate the initial context. They are not counts from a model's tokenizer, and they are not billed savings per request. Discovered schemas, search steps, history, and the provider's own serialization can add tokens later.

# CLAUDE.md - Testing Guide for OrcaSlicer

This guide provides comprehensive instructions for Claude Code when writing, maintaining, and understanding tests in the OrcaSlicer codebase.

## ⚠️ CRITICAL RULES - MUST FOLLOW

### 1. **SECTIONS IN LOOPS - NEVER REUSE NAMES**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause unpredictable behavior
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Bad loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        SECTION("Same name") {  // WRONG! Same name used multiple times
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use DYNAMIC_SECTION or incorporate counter
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Good loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        DYNAMIC_SECTION("Section " << i) {  // Unique name per iteration
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

### 2. **THREAD SAFETY - ASSERTIONS ARE NOT THREAD-SAFE**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([]() {
            REQUIRE(some_calculation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
        });
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Synchronize results, test on main thread
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    std::atomic<int> passed{0};
    
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([&passed]() {
            if (some_calculation() == expected) {
                passed++;
            }
        });
    }
    
    for (auto& t : threads) t.join();
    REQUIRE(passed == 4);  // Test results on main thread
}
```

### 3. **EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION - AVOID BINARY OPERATORS**
❌ **WRONG**: Cannot decompose properly
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0 && b < 10);  // Shows "false" on failure, not individual values
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Split into separate assertions
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0);
REQUIRE(b < 10);  // Each shows individual values on failure
```

### 4. **FLOATING POINT - NEVER USE APPROX**
❌ **WRONG**: Approx is deprecated and asymmetric
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_value == Catch::Approx(expected));  // Deprecated!
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use floating point matchers
```cpp
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));     // 4 ULPs apart
```

### 5. **TEST ORDERING - ALWAYS USE RANDOM ORDER**
✅ **REQUIRED**: For CI/CD and development
```bash
# Essential flags for running tests
./tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions

# For test sharding (parallel execution), share random seed
./tests --order rand --shard-index 0 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 1 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 2 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
```

## Overview of OrcaSlicer's Testing Framework

OrcaSlicer uses **Catch2 v3** (currently v3.11.0, vendored in `tests/catch2/`) as its primary testing framework. The test suite is organized into several modules that mirror the project's architectural components:

> **Note**: Test files include the framework via `#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>` (the v3 single-header convenience include). All v3 features described in this guide are available.

### Test Structure
```
tests/
├── CMakeLists.txt              # Main test configuration
├── catch_main.hpp              # Custom test reporter
├── libslic3r/                  # Core library tests (21 test files)
├── fff_print/                  # FFF printing tests (12 test files)
├── sla_print/                  # SLA printing tests (4 test files)
├── libnest2d/                  # 2D nesting tests
├── slic3rutils/               # Utility tests
├── data/                      # Test data files and meshes
└── catch2/                    # Catch2 framework files
```

### Build Integration
- Tests are built using CMake with `catch_discover_tests()` integration
- Each test module creates a separate executable (e.g., `libslic3r_tests`, `fff_print_tests`)
- Test data directory is available via `TEST_DATA_DIR` preprocessor definition
- Custom verbose console reporter provides detailed test output

## Test Suite Organization

### libslic3r Tests
Core slicing engine tests covering:
- **Geometry operations**: Points, polygons, lines, Voronoi diagrams
- **File formats**: STL, 3MF, AMF parsing and validation
- **Algorithms**: Clipper operations, mesh boolean operations, optimization
- **Configuration**: Print settings validation and parsing
- **Utilities**: String processing, time utilities, data structures

### fff_print Tests
Fused Filament Fabrication specific tests:
- **G-code generation**: Writer functionality, cooling, lift/unlift
- **Slicing algorithms**: Layer generation, infill patterns
- **Print mechanics**: Flow calculations, extrusion, support material
- **Model processing**: Print objects, skirt/brim generation

### sla_print Tests
Stereolithography specific tests:
- **SLA print processing**: Layer curing, support generation
- **Raycast operations**: Light path calculations
- **Test utilities**: SLA-specific helper functions

## Writing New Tests - Best Practices

### File Organization
1. **Naming Convention**: `test_<feature>.cpp` (e.g., `test_geometry.cpp`)
2. **Header Structure**: Include `<catch2/catch_all.hpp>` first, then relevant headers
3. **Namespace Usage**: Use `using namespace Slic3r;` for convenience
4. **File Placement**: Add to appropriate test directory and update CMakeLists.txt

### Test Naming and Structure
```cpp
#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>
#include "libslic3r/Point.hpp"

using namespace Slic3r;

TEST_CASE("Feature description", "[category_tag]") {
    // Test implementation
}
```

### Tagging System
Use descriptive tags for test categorization:
- `[Geometry]` - Geometric operations and calculations
- `[GCodeWriter]` - G-code generation functionality  
- `[Config]` - Configuration and settings tests
- `[FileFormat]` - File I/O operations (STL, 3MF, etc.)
- `[Algorithm]` - Core algorithms and processing
- `[Performance]` - Performance benchmarks (if applicable)

## Catch2 Features Guide

### Basic Assertions
```cpp
// Primary assertions - stop test on failure
REQUIRE(expression);
REQUIRE_FALSE(expression);

// Continuing assertions - continue test after failure  
CHECK(expression);
CHECK_FALSE(expression);

// Non-failing checks - record result but don't fail test
CHECK_NOFAIL(expression);  // Useful for assumptions that might be violated
```

### Exception Testing
```cpp
// Verify no exception is thrown
REQUIRE_NOTHROW(function_call());

// Verify any exception is thrown
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());

// Verify specific exception type
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(function_call(), SpecificException);

// Verify exception message
REQUIRE_THROWS_WITH(function_call(), "Expected error message");

// Verify exception with matchers (for partial matching)
REQUIRE_THROWS_MATCHES(function_call(), SpecificException, 
                       Catch::Matchers::Message("contains this"));
```

### Complex Assertions with Matchers
```cpp
#include <catch2/matchers/catch_matchers.hpp>

// String matchers
using Catch::Matchers::StartsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::EndsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::ContainsSubstring;
using Catch::Matchers::Equals;
using Catch::Matchers::Matches;  // Regex matching

REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, StartsWith("Expected prefix"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, ContainsSubstring("middle part"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, Matches(".*pattern.*"));

// Floating point matchers - ALWAYS use these instead of Approx!
using Catch::Matchers::WithinAbs;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinRel;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinULP;

REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));     // Absolute tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));      // Relative tolerance (1%)
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));         // ULP difference (requires IEEE-754)

// Combining matchers
REQUIRE_THAT(value, WithinRel(expected, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));
```

### Sections for Test Organization
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Complex feature testing", "[Feature]") {
    // Common setup code
    SomeObject obj;
    
    SECTION("First scenario") {
        // Specific test case
        REQUIRE(obj.method1() == expected_value);
    }
    
    SECTION("Second scenario") {
        // Another test case with same setup
        REQUIRE(obj.method2() == other_expected);
    }
}
```

### BDD-Style Tests
Use for complex scenarios and user story testing:

> **Note**: BDD macros are aliases for TEST_CASE and SECTION with prefixed names
```cpp
SCENARIO("User performs complex operation", "[UserStory]") {
    GIVEN("A specific setup condition") {
        GCodeWriter writer;
        // Setup code
        
        WHEN("User performs action") {
            auto result = writer.some_operation();
            
            THEN("Expected outcome occurs") {
                REQUIRE(result.size() > 0);
                
                AND_WHEN("Follow-up action occurs") {
                    auto next_result = writer.next_operation();
                    
                    THEN("Final outcome is correct") {
                        REQUIRE(next_result == expected);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### Data Generators for Parameterized Tests
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Function works with various inputs", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto test_value = GENERATE(1, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13);
    
    REQUIRE(is_odd(test_value));
    REQUIRE(test_value > 0);
}

// Range-based generators
TEST_CASE("Range testing", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto i = GENERATE(range(1, 10));  // 1 to 9
    REQUIRE(process_value(i) > i);
}

// Using variables in generators (requires GENERATE_COPY or GENERATE_REF)
TEST_CASE("Generator with variables", "[Algorithm]") {
    std::vector<int> values = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    auto test_value = GENERATE_REF(from_range(values));  // Use GENERATE_REF for references
    
    REQUIRE(test_value > 0);
}

// Custom generators
TEST_CASE("Random values", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto random_int = GENERATE(take(100, random(-1000, 1000)));  // 100 random values
    REQUIRE(process_random_value(random_int));
}
```

### Test Fixtures
```cpp
class GeometryFixture {
public:
    Point origin{0, 0};
    Point unit_x{1, 0};
    Point unit_y{0, 1};
    
    mutable double tolerance = EPSILON;  // Use mutable for data that might change
};

// Standard fixture - new instance per test run
TEST_CASE_METHOD(GeometryFixture, "Point operations", "[Geometry]") {
    REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_x) == 1.0);
}

// Persistent fixture - single instance for entire test case (v3.2.0+)
TEST_CASE_PERSISTENT_FIXTURE(GeometryFixture, "Persistent operations", "[Geometry]") {
    static int call_count = 0;
    ++call_count;
    INFO("This fixture persists across sections, call: " << call_count);
    
    SECTION("First section") {
        REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_x) == 1.0);
    }
    
    SECTION("Second section") {
        REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_y) == 1.0);
        // call_count will be 2 here with persistent fixture
```

## Common Pitfalls and Solutions

### Floating-Point Comparisons

> **CRITICAL**: Never use Approx - it's deprecated due to asymmetry and other issues

❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == expected_volume);           // Exact equality
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == Catch::Approx(expected));   // Deprecated! Asymmetric!
```

✅ **Correct**: Always use floating point matchers
```cpp
// Absolute tolerance - good when values are near zero
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinAbs(expected_volume, 0.001));

// Relative tolerance - good for values with different magnitudes
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance

// ULP (Units in Last Place) - most precise, requires IEEE-754
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinULP(expected_volume, 4));

// Combined approach - relative OR absolute
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, 
    WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));

// Precision control for output
Catch::StringMaker<double>::precision = 15;  // Show more decimal places
```

### Why Approx is Problematic:
- **Asymmetric**: `Approx(10).epsilon(0.1) != 11.1` but `Approx(11.1).epsilon(0.1) == 10`
- **Double-only**: All computation done in `double`, causes issues with `float` inputs  
- **Default behavior**: Only uses relative comparison, so `Approx(0) == X` only works for `X == 0`

### Path Handling
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
std::string path = TEST_DATA_DIR + "/model.obj";  // May have path separator issues
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
std::string path = std::string(TEST_DATA_DIR) + "/model.obj";
// or use boost::filesystem for complex path operations
```

### Exception Testing
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
bool threw_exception = false;
try {
    risky_function();
} catch (...) {
    threw_exception = true;
}
REQUIRE(threw_exception);
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());
// or for specific exceptions
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(risky_function(), SpecificException);
```

### Thread Safety

⚠️ **CRITICAL**: Catch2 assertions are **NOT thread-safe** by default!

> **Note**: Catch2 v3.9.0+ has opt-in thread-safe assertions via `CATCH_CONFIG_EXPERIMENTAL_THREAD_SAFE_ASSERTIONS`. OrcaSlicer is on v3.11.0 but does not enable this flag, so assertions remain non-thread-safe by default.

❌ **Incorrect**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
std::thread t([&]() {
    REQUIRE(threaded_operation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
    CHECK(other_operation());                   // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
});
```

✅ **Correct**: Collect results, assert on main thread
```cpp
std::atomic<bool> success{false};
std::atomic<int> error_count{0};

std::thread t([&]() {
    // Do work in thread, collect results
    bool result1 = (threaded_operation() == expected);
    bool result2 = other_operation();
    
    if (result1 && result2) {
        success = true;
    } else {
        error_count++;
    }
});

t.join();

// Assert results on main thread
REQUIRE(success);
REQUIRE(error_count == 0);
```

#### Thread Safety Rules:
- **REQUIRE family**: Would terminate process in spawned threads (throws exception with no try-catch)
- **CHECK family**: Not thread-safe, can corrupt internal state
- **SKIP, FAIL, SUCCEED**: Not thread-safe even with v3 thread-safe assertions
- **Message macros**: INFO, CAPTURE, WARN - not thread-safe
- **STATIC_REQUIRE/CHECK**: Not thread-safe (relies on runtime registration)

### Memory Management
Use RAII and smart pointers in tests:
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Resource management", "[Memory]") {
    auto model = std::make_unique<Model>();
    // Automatic cleanup on test completion/failure
    
    REQUIRE(model->objects.empty());
}
```

## Known Issues and Workarounds

### Platform-Specific Issues
```cpp
// MinGW/CygWin slow linking workaround
// Use: -fuse-ld=lld flag to speed up linking significantly
```

### Catch2 v3 Features Available

```cpp
// OrcaSlicer is on Catch2 v3.11.0 - all of these ARE available:
```

### workspace_inspect (line )
### settings_search (line 978)
"Find a page of process, object, filament or printer settings by key, label, or description. The query may hold several words or keys, and settings matching more of them come first. writable keeps only the settings the patch tools may change; changedOnly keeps only settings with unsaved changes (for object, the object's own overrides), which with an empty query lists every one. A page is not the full list; read known keys directly with settings_get or follow nextCursor."
### settings_get (line 985)
"Read current values and their preset origin; read before proposing a patch. process reads the values every object prints with. object reads the values that one object prints with: its own override where it has one (overridden: true), otherwise the process value. filament and printer read that preset: with its unsaved changes when it is the one being edited (differsFromPreset), otherwise as saved."
### settings_preview_patch (line 995)
"Validate an atomic settings patch, and persistAs, without changing anything; use the returned sessionId and revision when applying. A setting that holds one value per extruder or nozzle takes the same number of values, separated by commas. object checks the patch as overrides on that object: settings that apply to the whole print (skirt, travel speed, spiral vase and the like) are refused with unsupported_scope, and no dependencies are predicted because OrcaSlicer keeps object overrides as written. A filament or printer preset that is not the one being edited changes only by being saved (not_selected without persistAs)."
### settings_apply_patch (line 1001)
"Apply an atomic settings patch immediately. Requires the sessionId and revision from a preview of the same scope, target, changes and persistAs; edits to the model since that preview do not matter, a settings change does. A process, filament or printer change is not undone by project Undo; an object override is. With persistAs the preset is saved as well, and savedAs names what it was saved as."
### intent_update (line 1010)
"Record what the person said this print is for. setupTitle is the purpose in a few words. Each field is one requirement: field names it and value is what they said; assumed true marks one the person did not state, and question, in place of a value, records one still to ask. Send fields as an empty array for a title-only update. Project Undo does not undo this."
### plan_set (line 1021)
"State how you mean to print this project and why: the headline, one entry per decision with the alternative you rejected, what you assumed without being able to check, and what could still go wrong. Replaces the whole plan and runs immediately; project Undo does not undo this."
### presets_list (line 1332)
"List the presets of one kind this installation offers, newest compatibility verdict included. Compatible ones only unless you ask for all; a page is not the whole list, so follow nextCursor. Names are what a selection takes; labels are what the user sees."
### slice_report (line 1346)
"Read what a sliced plate says about itself, by section: summary is time and filament per extruder with weight and cost; findings are Orca's own warnings and errors (appliesWhen timelapse: only for a print that records a timelapse), the conflicts it detected, and whether a toolpath leaves the bed; material is filament and tool changes and the volume purged for them; supports lists support printed inside a hole of the mesh or inside a no_support or precision_hole region (with the support area summed over its layers); seams counts seams and how many landed on each face region that asks for or forbids them; firstLayer is the first layer height and each object's bed contact area and brim; island
### slice_start (line 1412)
"Start Orca's own slicing run for one plate, or every plate when you name none, and return once it has started; read the slicing section of workspace_inspect for the result, which is not ready then. With wait, return when the run ends instead (finished says whether the plates are sliced), which is what to use before reading slice_report. Fails when a slice is already running unless you pass preempt, because nothing records who started that run and it may be the user's."
### slice_inspect (line 1172)
"Expert detail of a sliced plate (default the active plate). view layers: per layer, from first (default 0), up to count (1 to 100) layers: height, time, extrusion roles, speed, fan, temperature and volumetric flow ranges, with layerCount and the next first to ask for. view gcode: the G-code text from line first (0-based), up to 64 KB, with the next first. A plate that has not been sliced says so."
### export_file (line 1196)
"Write a file to an absolute path the user chose: gcode (a sliced plate's G-code, .gcode), sliced_3mf (a sliced plate with its G-code, .3mf), project_3mf (the whole project, .3mf, without changing which file the project is), stl (objectIds, or a plate's objects, as placed, .stl), or presets (the printer, filament and process presets in use, as files in the folder path). plateId picks the plate for gcode, sliced_3mf and stl (default the active plate). === blind-calls predictions/notes ===
blind-calls: predictions, written before the first run and not edited afterwards.

What the earlier control records show (earlier\rewrite, a guide only): 22 refused calls, 13 of them
intent_update, object_analyze and presets_list; the typical shape is a call by name with no SEARCH in the
turn before it, a refusal, then a SEARCH and a good call, or two more guesses and the end of the turn.

search-first (explain that unloaded tools must be searched for before the first call in a turn):
- Blind refusals (a deferred tool called with no SEARCH earlier in the turn) fall several-fold against the
  control, most visibly for intent_update, object_analyze, presets_list.
- Runs ending in a failed turn fall (control expected around 4 of 12; this arm 0 to 2).
- outdoor-fitting: purpose recorded 3 of 3; ends on a PETG filament in at least 2 of 3. Ending sliced is the
  uncertain one: turn 3 still needs plan_set, printer_setup, the patch tools and slice_inspect, whose
  contracts are refused even after a search. I expect 1 or 2 of 3, not 3.
- Must not move: petg-question unchanged 3 of 3; what-is-this reads the shape and records the purpose 3 of 3;
  desk-ornament keeps its setup and ends sliced as often as the control.
- Cost: more SEARCH items, each of which brings schemas into the context, so input tokens per run go up
  somewhat (my guess: up to a third), partly paid back by fewer retries.

no-names (the instructions describe capabilities, name no deferred tool):
- Blind refusals of the three tools fall to near zero, because there is no name to call.
- The risk runs the other way: with no name the model may not look for the capability at all, or may invent a
  tool name (unknown_tool refusals). I expect what-is-this "read the shape" and "recorded the purpose" to
  hold at 2 or 3 of 3 but would not be surprised by a drop; a drop to 0 or 1 of 3 would be the cost of this arm.
- outdoor-fitting ends on PETG at least as often as the control; sliced uncertain, as above.
- petg-question unchanged 3 of 3.

loaded (control instructions; the six named tools sent with their parameters):
- Blind refusals of the six loaded tools are 0 by construction. What is left for those tools is the contract
  itself; I expect few (0 to 3 across 12 runs), mostly plan_set.
- Blind refusals move to the still-deferred tools the journey needs (printer_setup, settings_apply_patch,
  slice_inspect), so outdoor-fitting may still fail in turn 3, but later than in the control. PETG at
  least 2 of 3; sliced 1 to 3 of 3.
- desk-ornament kept and sliced 3 of 3; what-is-this 3 of 3 on both; petg-question unchanged 3 of 3.
- Cost: every request carries six more schemas (a fixed overhead per request), but fewer searches. Net input
  tokens about the same as the control, within a quarter either way.

Across all arms: if refusals of searched-for or loaded tools stay as common as blind ones were, the hypothesis
explains less of the failure than the brief supposes, and the contract (not the missing search) is the cause.

With the `namespaces` capability, JusPrin advertises six namespaces, and each has fewer than ten deferred functions. A deferred namespace shows its name and description at the start. On OpenAI a function that is deferred individually still shows its own name and description; only its parameters arrive with the search. On OpenRouter a deferred function is hidden entirely: its documentation says "the model cannot see or call one until a search returns it", and the first journey requests (about 2,650 input tokens with 26 functions deferred) agree.

**What deferral did to the journeys (2026-10-13).** The first version of deferral kept only three reads loaded and deferred the rest, including the `core` toolset that the catalog below calls "every turn". The instructions name `intent_update`, `object_analyze`, `presets_list`, `plan_set`, `slice_report`, `slice_inspect` and `export_file`. On OpenRouter, where a deferred function is invisible, DeepSeek V4 Flash called those tools by the name it had read, without searching for them, so without their parameters: `intent_update` with `requirements`, `presets_list` with `category`, `object_analyze` with no `include`. The adapter refuses a call whose arguments miss the schema, and the third refusal in a turn ends the turn. In twelve runs of the four scenarios, 20 of 25 refused calls were such guesses, three runs ended that way, and the preparation scenario never reached a slice. Sending the six named tools loaded took refusals of those tools from 19 of 59 calls to 0 of 61 and all refusals from 25 to 5; a paragraph telling the model to search first did not stop the guesses; and removing the names from the instructions removed the behaviours with them (the model did not go looking for tools it was not told about). Loading the named tools is therefore the fix, not rewording. The records and method are in `tests/project_journey/README.md`. The built-in OpenAI route hides the function inside a namespace just as completely, and it has not yet been run on these journeys.

They are not app tools and they never reach the coordinator. Across user turns, the app replays its own history of calls and results, and gives each function its current namespace. entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

Interim summary of what the evidence says, in plain terms:

- **What went wrong.** The deferral commit hid every tool except three reads behind the provider's tool search, but the assistant's instructions still name seven tools by name. On OpenRouter a hidden tool is completely invisible, so the model did the natural thing: it called the tool it had just been told to use, guessed the argument names, and was refused. Three refusals end the turn. The commit also deferred the whole "core" toolset that the guide's own catalog describes as needed on every turn.
- **The fix.** Keep deferral, but load every tool the instructions name plus the core set (13 tools loaded, 16 still deferred), and add a unit test that fails if anyone names a deferred tool in the instructions again. The six-tool version of this change has already been measured live: refusals of those tools went from 19 of 59 calls to none.
- **Keeping search results across turns** is not worth building: in sixty recorded runs, only one of 212 searches re-found a tool an earlier turn had already found.
- **The OpenAI route** has never been journeyed. I added a harness switch for it; running it needs your approval, which I'll ask for with numbers once the build and unit tests pass.

content.text:
Everything that can be done without a live model call is done, so I'm stopping here to ask for approval of the live runs.

## What was wrong

The deferral commit hid every tool except three reads behind the provider's tool search, but the assistant's instructions still tell the model to call seven tools by name (intent_update, object_analyze, presets_list, plan_set, slice_report, slice_inspect, export_file). On OpenRouter a deferred tool is invisible: OpenRouter's guide says the model "cannot see or call one until a search returns it". So the model did the obvious thing with a name it had just read: it called it, invented argument names, and the app refused the call. Three refusals end the turn. The records show exactly this shape in run after run: a call with no search before it, a refusal, then either a search and a correct call, or two more guesses and a dead turn. Telling the model to search first did not help, and removing the names removed the behaviours the names drive. The commit also deferred the whole "core" toolset that the guide's own catalog describes as needed on every turn, which is why even a successful run spent five to eight searches finding tools it needs every time.

Keeping search results across turns, the other candidate fix, would have bought almost nothing: in sixty recorded deferral runs, only one of 212 searches re-found a tool an earlier turn had already found. I did not build it.

## The fix (uncommitted in the worktree, branch `claude/deferral-fix`)

- `deferred_toolsets()` in [OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp:76](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp:76) now loads the core set plus the three other named tools: 13 loaded, 16 deferred in six namespaces. The rule is stated in the comment: a tool the instructions name, or a loaded tool's description names, is loaded.
- A new test, "every tool the instructions name is loaded", scans the real instruction text and the loaded descriptions and fails if a named tool is deferred. It immediately caught one: object_analyze's description named region_annotate, so I reworded that clause. All 281 agent tests pass.
- Cost: the first request's tool context grows from about 5 KB to about 17.6 KB, so deferral now saves about 4,100 tokens on an uncached request instead of 7,200. From the recorded runs, the first OpenRouter request should land near 7,500 input tokens versus 11,800 with deferral off and 4,200 before the fix. Later requests are mostly cached.
- The guide and the journey README describe the mechanism and the new numbers. The harness gained `JUSPRIN_JOURNEY_ROUTE=app` so the same scenarios can run on the app's own OpenAI route. The harness built from this tree launches, renders, and completes the Agent page handshake with no key set.

Note that jusprin-newui now carries your revert of the deferral commit, and another session is mid-merge in the main checkout, so I touched nothing there. Landing this means re-applying the deferral commit together with these changes.

## Live runs that need your approval

1. **DeepSeek on OpenRouter, the judging route, 12 runs** (three per scenario) with the fix. Estimate from the closest recorded arm: about 2 million input tokens (roughly 60 percent cached), 70 thousand output, about $0.20 at list price. The before side already exists: the twelve control runs from 2026-10-13.
2. **The app's own route, gpt-5.4-mini with namespaces, 8 runs**: one of each scenario with the old three-tool loading and one with the fix. This answers whether the shipping default has the same failure, which has never been measured. Estimate about 1.3 million input tokens and 50 thousand output, under about $1.50 at the listed $0.75 per million input and $4.50 per million output ([pricing source](https://pricepertoken.com/pricing-page/model/openai-gpt-5.4-mini), [second source](https://anotherwrapper.com/llm-pricing/gpt-5.4-mini)).

Say which batches to run, and I'll run them one app at a time, log every request's usage, and write the results into the journey README.

I found no primary Anthropic evaluation page in these results. Everything below comes from secondary sources that report on Anthropic's figures or run their own tests.

**Anthropic's reported numbers.** Secondary coverage says Anthropic's internal MCP evaluation showed higher tool-selection accuracy with deferred loading. One write-up gives Opus 4 going from 49% to 74%, and Opus 4.5 going from 79.5% to 88.1% (Medium). A second report repeats the same two pairs and notes they were published on 24 November 2025 (Unity Horizon).

**Independent tests.** Arcade.dev tested Tool Search with about 4,000 tools across 25 workflows. It measured retrieval only, meaning whether the right tool appeared in the search results, not whether Claude then selected it (Arcade). Its reported averages were 56% for regex and 64% for BM25 (Growth Method).

**A competitor comparison.** Stacklok ran its own head-to-head test using Claude Sonnet 4.5. It reported Tool Search at roughly 34% selection accuracy and 48% retrieval accuracy with BM25, against its own MCP Optimizer at about 94% and 98% (DEV Community). Because this comes from a vendor with a stake in the result, treat it with caution.

**Caveats on the evidence.** One critique notes that the Anthropic figures come from a vendor measuring its own feature on an evaluation others cannot run, and that repeated runs of a different benchmark varied widely (Unity Horizon). The Arcade numbers are also older, and Anthropic's search implementations may have changed since.

To verify the official figures, check Anthropic's own engineering blog and the Tool Search documentation on the Claude Developer Platform directly. I can run another search targeting those pages if you want.
